Otherwise relax neighbors and offer new entries when you improve a distance.  Example code:  public class Node {     public final char label;     public final Map<Node,Integer> neighbours = new LinkedHashMap<>();     public Node(char label) { this.label = label; }     public void addNeighbour(Node n, int w) { neighbours.put(n, w); }     @Override public boolean equals(Object o){ return (o instanceof Node) && ((Node)o).label==label; }     @Override public int hashCode(){ return Character.hashCode(label); } }  static class Entry {     final Node node;     final int dist;     Entry(Node n, int d){ node = n; dist = d; } }  public static Map<Node,Integer> dijkstra(Node source) {     Map<Node,Integer> best = new HashMap<>();     PriorityQueue<Entry> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparingInt(e -> e.dist));     best.put(source, 0);     pq.offer(new Entry(source, 0));     Set<Node> visited = new HashSet<>(); // optional; you can also rely on best map + stale check      while (!pq.isEmpty()) {         Entry e = pq.poll(); This approach is simple, correct, and commonly used in Java.

}      @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {         return (o instanceof Node) && label.equals(((Node)o).label);     }     @Override public int hashCode() { return label.hashCode(); }     @Override public String toString() { return label; } }  static class PQEntry implements Comparable<PQEntry> {     final Node node;     final int dist;     PQEntry(Node node, int dist) { this.node = node; this.dist = dist; }     @Override public int compareTo(PQEntry o) { return Integer.compare(this.dist, o.dist); } }  public void dijkstra(Node source) {     PriorityQueue<PQEntry> pq = new PriorityQueue<>();     source.setDistance(0);     pq.add(new PQEntry(source, 0));      while (!pq.isEmpty()) {         PQEntry e = pq.poll();         Node u = e.node;         // stale entry check         if (e.dist != u.getDistance()) continue;          for (Map.Entry<Node,Integer> me : u.neighbors.entrySet()) {             Node v = me.getKey();             int w = me.getValue();             int nd = u.getDistance() + w;             if (nd < v.getDistance()) {                 v.setDistance(nd);                 pq.add(new PQEntry(v, nd)); // push updated snapshot             }         }     } }  Notes - This avoids trying to remove or mutate elements already in the heap (PriorityQueue has no decrease-key). - Complexity: O((V + E) log V). - If you need explicit decrease-key (avoid duplicate entries), implement an indexed binary heap (store node -> index) or use a specialized library (Fibonacci heap / indexed priority queue).

1|55:	That error means Cargo couldn’t find any executable target (a crate with a main function) in the directory you invoked it from. burn is a library/workspace, so running from the workspace root (or a library crate) gives that message. Don’t have nested [workspace] roots — either include sub-crates as members of the parent workspace or reference them with path dependencies.  How to do it (practical steps):  1. Create a library crate: - cargo new common_lib --lib - edit common_lib/src/lib.rs and common_lib/Cargo.toml (name, version, edition).  2. Create other crates (libraries or bins): - cargo new bigger_lib --lib - cargo new my_app --bin  3. Create a workspace at the repository root (one Cargo.toml): [workspace] members = ["my_app", "common_lib", "bigger_lib"]  This makes all members share one Cargo.lock and build directory and allows crates to depend on each other by name without specifying path in each member.  4. Major benefits of using secondary data are: faster and cheaper access to information than primary collection (Saunders, Lewis & Thornhill 2019); the ability to analyse large, representative or longitudinal samples that would be impractical for an individual researcher to gather (Hox & Boeije 2005); opportunities for comparative and trend analyses across time or populations; and ethical/feasibility advantages when direct data collection is sensitive or impossible (Heaton 2004; Saunders, Lewis & Thornhill 2019). Secondary data also supports method triangulation and hypothesis testing, increasing robustness when combined carefully with primary data (Bryman 2016).   Key caveats are limited control over measurement, possible mismatch with your research questions, unknown quality or biases, and issues of missing variables or documentation; these require careful provenance checks, metadata review, sensitivity analyses and, where needed, reweighting or harmonisation (Hox & Boeije 2005; Bryman 2016). In practice, treat secondary datasets as research instruments: evaluate their origin, sampling frame, collection methods and metadata before reuse, and document those assessments in your write-up (Umeå University Library n.d.; Bryman 2016).

Minimal example (conceptual) - This example uses AlQuran.cloud to fetch Surah 1 and displays it in a read-only QTextEdit.  package main  import (     "encoding/json"     "net/http"     "os"     "strings"      "github.com/therecipe/qt/core"     "github.com/therecipe/qt/widgets" )  func fetchSurahHTML(surahID int) (string, error) {     url := "https://api.alquran.cloud/v1/surah/" +             strings.TrimSpace(strings.TrimSuffix(strings.TrimPrefix(strings.TrimSpace(strings.Trim(fmt.Sprint(surahID), " ")), " "), " "), "") +            "/ar.alafasy"     resp, err := http.Get(url)     if err != nil { return "", err }     defer resp.Body.Close()      var body struct {         Data struct {             Ayahs []struct {                 Number int    `json:"number"`                 Text   string `json:"text"`             } `json:"ayahs"`         } `json:"data"`     }     if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&body); err != nil { return "", err }      // Build RTL HTML. Use a trusted Arabic font installed on the system.     html := `<div dir="rtl" style="font-family: 'Scheherazade', 'Noto Naskh Arabic', serif; font-size:28px;">`     for _, a := range body.Data.Ayahs {         html += "<p>" + core.QCoreApplication_Translate("", a.Text) + "</p>"     }     html += "</div>"     return html, nil }  func main() {     app := widgets.NewQApplication(len(os.Args), os.Args)      html, err := fetchSurahHTML(1) // fetch Surah Al-Fatiha     if err != nil {         // handle error (show message, etc.)         html = "<p>Error fetching</p>"     }      win := widgets.NewQMainWindow(nil, 0)     win.SetWindowTitle("Quran Reader")     te := widgets.NewQTextEdit(nil)     te.SetReadOnly(true)     te.SetLayoutDirection(core.Qt__RightToLeft) // ensures widget layout is RTL     te.SetHtml(html)      win.SetCentralWidget(te)     win.Show()     app.Exec() }  Notes and practical tips - Fonts: install a proper Arabic font (Noto Naskh, Scheherazade) and reference it in the HTML/CSS so shaping and diacritics render correctly. - RTL: set widget layout direction and use dir="rtl" in HTML. - Tajweed coloring: best options are (a) obtain a pre-colored mushaf or (b) implement rule-based coloring on the server/client (complex). 1|66:	Easiest reliable method: make a curve that matches the slide, use a Follow Path setup for the camera, and add a tracking/empty for orientation and shake. Steps:  1. Create the path - Add > Curve > Bezier (or Path). Edit its control points in Edit Mode so the curve follows the slide from top to bottom.  2. Attach the camera to the path - Select the camera, go to Constraints > Add Object Constraint > Follow Path, set the Target to the curve. - Enable "Follow Curve" (or "Follow" depending on Blender version) so the camera rotates with the path. Set Forward/Up axes so the camera points correctly (try Forward = -Z, Up = Y).  3. Animate the motion - Animate the constraint's Offset/Offset Factor from 0 to 1 (or animate the curve’s Evaluation Time if using a Path object) across the frames you want. Keyframe start and end; adjust timing in the Graph Editor (linear for constant speed, ease for acceleration/deceleration).  4. Control where the camera looks - Add an Empty at the slide’s focal point (or a character). Use a Track To or Damped Track constraint on the camera targeting that Empty so the camera keeps a stable aim while sliding. - Alternatively parent the camera to an Empty that follows the path and rotate the camera relative to that Empty.  5. Add shake and polish - For subtle shake, parent a small-animated Empty to the camera (or add a Noise modifier to the camera’s location/rotation F-curves) and keyframe tiny offsets. - Tweak field of view, depth of field, motion blur, and interpolation in the Graph Editor to get the feeling of speed and weight.  Tips - If you want physically plausible speed, edit the speed curve in the Graph Editor rather than changing the path. - Use an Empty as an intermediary for easier orientation tweaking. - Use a Path object and its built-in Path Animation if you prefer auto keyframing via the curve’s Frames/Evaluation Time.  This workflow is simple, flexible, and lets you refine speed, rotation and camera aim without remodeling the slide.
2|66:	Easiest and most reliable method: make a curve that follows the slide, constrain the camera to that curve, then animate the curve offset. Steps:  1. Model or place your slide mesh.   2. Add a curve (Add → Curve → Bezier) and edit it in Edit Mode so its path runs down the inside of the slide (use handles to match the turns). Optionally set tilt on curve control points to control camera roll/banking.   3. Add a Camera and place it at the start of the curve.   4. Select the Camera → Constraints tab → Add Constraint → Follow Path. Set the Target to your curve and enable “Follow Curve” (and adjust Forward/Up axes so the camera points along the path).   5. Animate the motion: with the camera selected, keyframe the constraint’s Offset Factor (or Offset) from 0 (start) to 1 (end) across the frames you want. Alternatively enable the curve’s Path Animation and keyframe Evaluation Time.   6. To keep the camera looking at a point or smoothing orientation, add a Track To (or Damped Track) constraint targeting an Empty placed ahead on the path (or parent an Empty to the curve and move it along the path).   7. Add realism: use the Graph Editor to tweak easing (accelerate at start for gravity), add a Noise modifier for subtle camera shake, or parent an Empty to the camera and animate small positional keyframes.   8. Set render/output settings and render animation.  This method is simple, non-physical, and gives full control over timing, roll, and look direction without complex simulations.
3|66:	Best quick method: make a curve that follows the slide, then drive the camera along that curve with a Follow Path constraint (optionally parent the camera to an Empty for extra control). Steps:  1. Create the path  - Add → Curve → Bezier (or use another curve type). In Edit Mode shape the curve to match the slide (use snapping to vertices/faces to snap points to the slide mesh).  2. Position the camera  - Place the camera at the start of the slide and orient it roughly how you want the view (camera’s -Z is forward).  3. Make the camera follow the curve  - Select the camera → Constraints tab → Add Constraint → Follow Path. Set Target to the curve.  - Enable Follow Curve (so the camera orients along the tangent). Set Forward = -Z and Up = Y (camera’s forward is -Z).  - If you want the camera to exactly stick to the curve position, enable Fixed Position.  4. Animate the motion  - Animate the Offset Factor (or Offset/Evaluation Time depending on Blender version) from 0 to 1 (or from start frame to end frame): right‑click → Insert Keyframe at start and end frames.  - In the Graph Editor set interpolation to Linear for constant speed or adjust curves for easing.  5. Extra control (recommended)  - Parent camera to an Empty, then constrain the Empty to the curve instead of the camera. This makes it easy to add roll/banking by rotating the Empty while the Empty follows the path.  - Use a Track To or Damped Track constraint on the camera to keep it looking at a subject or an Empty target.  - Add subtle shake by animating a small Noise modifier on the Empty’s location/rotation f-curves (Graph Editor → Add Modifier → Noise).  6. Polish for realism  - Enable motion blur in Render Properties and add Depth of Field on the camera for cinematic feel.  - Tweak curve resolution or add helpers to avoid sudden orientation flips; use small control points to keep a smooth path.  This workflow is fast, non-destructive, gives straight control over timing, and lets you add roll/banking and shake without altering the path itself.

Define goal and approach    - Decide whether you want text-to-video, image-to-video (animate references), or to fine-tune a model to reproduce a specific subject/style (embedding / LoRA / DreamBooth-like approach).  2. Gather and prepare data    - Collect high-quality source videos and any paired text prompts/annotations. For subject-specific training, collect many varied clips showing the subject in different poses, lighting, and angles.    - Extract frames (and audio if needed). Start small and validate frequently to avoid overfitting.    - Use temporal consistency losses / conditioning (optical flow, temporal attention) if available to preserve motion coherence.    - If audio is relevant, include an audio-visual alignment loss or separate audio model.  6. Define the goal and choose a framework  - Decide whether you want to (a) learn an embedding (e.g., a face token), (b) fine‑tune an image or video model, or (c) train a model that models temporal dynamics (flow/latent temporal module). Pick a compatible framework (Automatic1111 embeddings, Stable Diffusion finetuning pipelines, or a video model training pipeline).  2. Collect and preprocess video data  - Use licensed/consented clips and diverse examples covering poses, lighting, expressions, and backgrounds.  - Extract frames at an appropriate rate (e.g., 1–10 fps for appearance datasets; higher for motion modeling).  - Convert problematic formats (WebP → PNG/JPEG), ensure resolution >=512×512 where possible, and keep consistent aspect ratio.  - Crop/align subjects (face alignment if training a face embedding), remove frames with occlusions or watermarks, and optionally upscale low‑res frames (GFPGAN/ESRGAN).  3. Build the dataset and annotations  - Organize folders of frames and, if needed, accompanying metadata: prompts, text captions, masks, optical flow, or per‑frame pose landmarks.  - Create train/validation splits to detect overfitting.  4. Start small for embeddings (low lr, few hundred–thousand steps); larger for full finetune.  - Use augmentations and regularization to avoid overfitting.  5. Monitor and validate  - Track training loss and validation loss (TensorBoard or equivalent), and inspect generated frames and short clips frequently.  - Use human evaluation or benchmarks for video tasks (visual quality, prompt alignment, temporal consistency, audio sync if applicable).  6. Practical tips  - Use many high‑quality, varied images rather than many similar frames to learn appearance; use consecutive frames when learning motion.  - Minimum useful resolution: ~512×512 for many diffusion pipelines.  - Convert WebP to PNG to avoid compatibility problems.  - Adjust training steps and lr to prevent overfitting; use validation early stopping.  - For faces, an embedding file stores the learned facial features and can be reused to apply that identity to other models.  Ethics and legality  - Ensure you have the rights and consent to train on people’s images and respect copyright and privacy laws.  This approach generalizes across image and video generators (Stable Diffusion, Veo‑style pipelines, and similar).

1|73:	Best way (most reliable, restaurant-quality): sous-vide at 125°F (52°C), then finish with a high‑heat sear.  Why: sous‑vide gives precise temperature control so the flesh never overcooks, stays moist and tender, and preserves flavor/omega‑3s; the quick sear crisps the skin and adds Maillard flavor.  How (simple): - Season fillets; vacuum‑seal or use a zip‑top bag with most air removed. - Cook sous‑vide at 125°F (52°C) for 30–45 minutes (longer for very thick pieces). - Remove, pat dry, and sear skin‑side down in a hot oiled pan 30–60 seconds to crisp skin (or torch briefly). - Rest 1–2 minutes and serve. 2|73:	Best overall method for reliably moist, flavorful salmon (home cooks): pan-sear skin-side down to crisp the skin, then finish in a hot oven until the thickest part reaches 125–130°F (52–54°C); rest 4–5 minutes before serving. Why this works - Searing crisps the skin and protects the flesh; oven finishing gives even cooking without overcooking.   - 125–130°F yields tender, moist, slightly translucent salmon; higher temps (≥145°F) give a firmer, flakier, drier result.   - Use a probe thermometer for consistent results; if serving immunocompromised people or pregnant guests, follow FDA guidance (145°F).  If you have sous‑vide gear, cooking at ~50–52°C (122–125°F) produces the most precise, foolproof texture.

1|75:	Yes — you can reproduce that FiveM volleyball behavior. The cleanest, reliable approach is to build a FiveM resource with server-authoritative ball physics and client-side input/animation + interpolation for smoothness. Below is a concise plan, needed pieces, and minimal example snippets to get you started.  High-level design - Resource type: FiveM (Cfx.re) resource (Lua or JS; Lua recommended for quick prototyping). - Authority: Server is authoritative for the ball’s state (position, velocity, score). Clients send hit intents; server validates and applies physics. - Clients: handle player input, play animations, show the ball, and interpolate the server state for smooth movement. - Natives/APIs to use: NetworkRegisterEntityAsNetworked / NetworkGetNetworkIdFromEntity / NetworkSetEntityOwner, SetEntityVelocity / GetEntityVelocity, ApplyForceToEntity or SetEntityCoordsNoOffset for corrections, Raycast/ShapeTest or IsEntityTouchingEntity for collision detection, TaskPlayAnim for player hits.  Required assets & dev tasks 1. Ball model: use a GTA prop (e.g., prop_beach_volball01) or import custom model. Spawn it as a networked object. 2. Net model: static object or model placed in world. 3. Animations: use built-in GTA anims for hits/serves or import custom ones. 4. UI: score display, timers. 5. Match rules: serve, volley, detection of floor side/out, scoring.  Core workflow (server + client) 1. On match start, server spawns ball as networked entity and broadcasts its network ID. 2. Clients attach local visuals to that entity, interpolate position from server updates. 3. When a client hits the ball:    - Client detects hit input and local proximity/angle, plays hit animation and sends a server event with hit vector and a small signature (speed, timestamp).    - Server validates (player close enough, cooldown, allowed state) then sets ball velocity (SetEntityVelocity) or ApplyForceToEntity and updates authoritative state. 4. Server runs a physics tick (e.g., 50 ms) to read ball position/velocity and broadcast state to clients. Clients smoothly interpolate between updates. 5. Collision with ground: server detects ball touching ground via raycast/IsEntityTouchingEntity or by checking z coordinate crossing; determine which side it hit and award point, then respawn/serve. 6. 1|72:	Short answer (clinical viewpoint) Heart failure (HF) is a clinical syndrome in which structural or functional cardiac abnormalities cause the heart to be unable to provide adequate cardiac output and/or accommodate venous return, producing typical symptoms (dyspnea, fatigue, exercise intolerance) and signs (pulmonary crackles, raised jugular venous pressure, peripheral edema) together with objective evidence of cardiogenic pulmonary or systemic congestion.  When to call it heart failure - Require: typical symptoms and/or signs PLUS objective evidence of cardiac dysfunction or congestion (per the 2021 Universal Definition).   - Objective tests commonly used: elevated natriuretic peptide (BNP or NT‑proBNP), chest X‑ray showing congestion, and cardiac imaging (echocardiography showing reduced ejection fraction, structural abnormality, or elevated filling pressures).   - Classification by LVEF: HFrEF ≤40%, HFmrEF 41–49%, HFpEF ≥50%. Also acute vs chronic, left vs right.  Common causes - Ischemic heart disease / prior myocardial infarction (most common).   - Hypertension (longstanding pressure overload).   - Cardiomyopathies (dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive).   - Valvular heart disease (stenosis or regurgitation).   - Arrhythmias (e.g., tachycardia‑induced cardiomyopathy).   - Metabolic disease (diabetes), infections, toxins (alcohol, drugs), congenital defects.   - Risk factors that predispose to HF: obesity, smoking, sleep apnea, chronic kidney disease.  How systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) can cause heart failure SLE can cause HF by several mechanisms, often acting together: - Myocarditis: autoimmune inflammation of myocardium → impaired contractility → HFrEF; may be focal or diffuse.   - Coronary involvement: accelerated atherosclerosis from chronic inflammation and steroid use, coronary vasculitis or thrombosis (especially with antiphospholipid antibodies) → ischemia/MI → HF.   - Valvular disease: Libman–Sacks (nonbacterial) endocarditis or inflammatory damage → significant regurgitation → volume overload/HF.   - Pericarditis with effusion or tamponade → acute hemodynamic compromise.   - Pulmonary hypertension (from lung disease or thromboembolic disease) → right HF.   - Renal involvement (lupus nephritis) → volume overload and worsening HF.   Clinical implication: in a patient with SLE and new dyspnea, evaluate for myocarditis, ischemia, valvular disease, volume overload and screen for antiphospholipid syndrome.  Workup (practical) - History and exam focused on HF signs and SLE activity.   - BNP/NT‑proBNP, CBC, electrolytes, renal and liver function, troponin if ischemia suspected.   - ECG and chest X‑ray.   - Echocardiogram (first‑line imaging for structure and LVEF).   - Cardiac MRI if myocarditis suspected.   - Coronary angiography if ischemia likely.   - For SLE: ANA/dsDNA, complement levels, antiphospholipid antibodies, and assessment of renal function/urinalysis. Endomyocardial biopsy rarely, when diagnosis is uncertain.  Management principles 1) Treat the HF syndrome (general guideline-based therapy) - Acute decompensation: IV loop diuretics, oxygen as needed, vasodilators if hypertensive, inotropes for hypoperfusion, consider mechanical support if refractory.   - Chronic HFrEF foundational drugs (reduce symptoms and mortality): ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) or ACE inhibitor/ARB, beta‑blocker, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA), SGLT2 inhibitor; loop diuretics for volume control.   - In HFpEF/HFmrEF: manage congestion (diuretics) and optimize comorbidities; SGLT2 inhibitors now have a role across EF ranges.   - Device therapy for selected patients: ICD for primary prevention if low EF, CRT for dyssynchrony; advanced options—ventricular assist devices, transplantation.  2) Treat underlying causes and SLE‑specific therapy - If SLE myocarditis or active inflammatory cardiac involvement: treat the autoimmune process (high‑dose corticosteroids often first‑line; add other immunosuppressants—e.g., mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide, azathioprine—guided by severity and specialist input).   - Manage coronary disease (revascularization when indicated) and aggressive risk‑factor control (lipids, blood pressure, smoking cessation).   - Treat valvular disease surgically or percutaneously when severe.   - Anticoagulate when antiphospholipid syndrome or thromboembolism is present.   - Adjust HF pharmacotherapy for renal function and drug interactions with immunosuppressants.  3) General measures and monitoring - Sodium restriction, fluid management, structured exercise/rehabilitation, vaccination, weight monitoring, smoking/alcohol cessation.   - Regular follow up with BNP, renal electrolytes, echocardiography as indicated. Coordinate cardiology and rheumatology care for SLE patients.  Prognosis and prevention - Prognosis depends on cause, EF, comorbidities, and response to therapy. Early detection, treating SLE activity, and guideline‑directed HF therapy improve outcomes. Preventive measures include optimal control of blood pressure, lipids, glucose, smoking cessation, and timely treatment of SLE flares. 2|72:	Summary definition - Heart failure (HF) is a clinical syndrome in which structural or functional cardiac abnormalities cause the heart to fail to deliver adequate cardiac output and/or produce elevated filling pressures, producing typical symptoms (dyspnea, fatigue) and signs (pulmonary rales, elevated jugular venous pressure, peripheral edema).  When to call it heart failure (diagnostic approach) - Clinical: compatible symptoms ± signs (dyspnea on exertion/at rest, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, edema, fatigue). - Objective confirmation (required): elevated natriuretic peptide (BNP/NT‑proBNP) and/or imaging evidence of cardiac dysfunction (echocardiography showing reduced LVEF, impaired diastolic function, structural heart disease, or elevated filling pressures). - Classify by left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF): HFrEF ≤40%, HFmrEF 41–49%, HFpEF ≥50%. - Acute vs chronic: acute decompensated HF presents suddenly and needs urgent stabilization.  Common causes - Ischemic heart disease (coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction) - Longstanding hypertension - Cardiomyopathies (dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive) - Valvular heart disease - Arrhythmias (tachycardia‑mediated or bradyarrhythmias) - Metabolic contributors: diabetes, obesity, thyroid disease - Renal dysfunction, anemia, alcohol/toxin‑related damage  How systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) can cause heart failure SLE can lead to HF by multiple mechanisms; in an SLE patient with symptoms/signs suggestive of HF, consider: - Myocarditis: immune‑mediated inflammation of myocardium → systolic dysfunction and HF. - Premature/accelerated coronary atherosclerosis and coronary thrombosis (including antiphospholipid syndrome) → ischemic cardiomyopathy. - Valvular disease (Libman–Sacks endocarditis, regurgitation) → volume overload and HF. - Pericardial disease/tamponade causing impaired filling. - Pulmonary hypertension (from pulmonary vascular disease or chronic thromboembolism) → right HF. - Renal lupus (lupus nephritis) → volume overload, hypertension, and uremic cardiomyopathy. - Systemic inflammation, anemia, and corticosteroid‑related metabolic effects that worsen cardiac function. Acute stabilization (if decompensated)    - Oxygen, diuretics for congestion, vasodilators or inotropes if needed, treat arrhythmias, treat tamponade if present.  2. Guideline‑directed chronic HF therapy (tailored to LVEF)    - For HFrEF: neurohormonal blockade with ARNI (or ACE inhibitor/ARB), beta‑blocker, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, SGLT2 inhibitor; diuretics for symptom control; device therapy (CRT/ICD) when indicated.    - For HFpEF: treat congestion with diuretics, manage comorbidities (BP, AF, ischemia, obesity); SGLT2 inhibitors have benefit in many patients with HFpEF.    - Manage triggers: correct arrhythmias, ischemia, anemia, thyroid disease, fluid/ salt restrictions, rehabilitation/exercise.  3. Treat underlying SLE activity (essential in SLE‑related HF)    - For myocarditis or active inflammatory cardiac disease: prompt immunosuppression (high‑dose corticosteroids ± additional agents such as azathioprine, mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide or biologics depending on severity and specialist guidance).    - For valvular lesions or thrombotic disease: surgical or percutaneous repair when indicated; anticoagulation for antiphospholipid syndrome.    - For pericarditis/tamponade: antiinflammatory therapy and drainage when required.    - Manage lupus nephritis and hypertension to reduce volume overload and cardiac stress.  4. Follow‑up and multidisciplinary care    - Cardiology + rheumatology coordination.    - Monitor cardiac function (serial echocardiography, biomarkers), SLE activity, renal function, and drug adverse effects (immunosuppressants, HF medications).    - Vaccination, lifestyle measures (sodium restriction, smoking cessation, exercise), cardiac rehabilitation.  When to refer urgently - New or worsening HF symptoms, hemodynamic instability, suspected myocarditis, tamponade, severe pulmonary hypertension, or refractory HF despite therapy — urgent cardiology and rheumatology input.  Bottom line - Diagnose HF when compatible symptoms/signs are supported by elevated natriuretic peptides or imaging evidence of cardiac dysfunction. The current (2021) Universal Definition requires symptoms/signs plus a structural/functional heart abnormality and/or corroborative biomarkers (e.g., elevated BNP/NT‑proBNP) or imaging (echocardiographic evidence of reduced EF, abnormal filling pressures, valve disease, etc.). - HF can be acute or chronic and is subclassified by left‑ventricular ejection fraction: HFrEF (≤40%), HFmrEF (41–49%), HFpEF (≥50%).  When to say “this is heart failure” - Clinical suspicion: patient has typical symptoms (exertional or orthopneic dyspnea, fatigue, edema, reduced exercise tolerance) and signs of congestion. - Confirm when you have at least one objective finding: elevated natriuretic peptide, chest x‑ray showing pulmonary congestion, and/or echocardiography showing reduced EF, diastolic dysfunction, raised filling pressures or structural abnormalities. - Always exclude alternative causes of symptoms (pulmonary disease, anemia, thyroid disease) and consider acute triggers (ischemia, arrhythmia, infection, uncontrolled BP, fluid overload). Bottom line: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome diagnosed by typical symptoms/signs plus objective evidence of cardiac dysfunction or congestion. Also note acute vs chronic, left- vs right-sided, and systolic vs diastolic dysfunction.  Common causes - Ischemic heart disease (coronary artery disease, prior MI) - Longstanding hypertension - Valvular heart disease - Primary cardiomyopathies (dilated, restrictive, hypertrophic) - Arrhythmias (e.g., tachycardia‑mediated) - Diabetes, obesity, smoking, alcohol misuse, sleep apnea - Congenital heart disease  How systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) can cause HF - Myocarditis: immune‑mediated inflammatory injury of myocardium → systolic dysfunction. - Premature atherosclerosis: accelerated CAD in SLE → ischemia/MI → ischemic cardiomyopathy. - Valvular involvement (Libman‑Sacks endocarditis) or severe regurgitation → volume overload and HF. - Pulmonary hypertension from pulmonary vascular disease → right‑sided HF. - Pericardial disease (recurrent pericarditis, constriction, rarely tamponade) → impaired filling and HF signs. - Therapies and comorbidities: long‑term steroids and some cytotoxic drugs can worsen hypertension, dyslipidemia or be cardiotoxic, increasing HF risk. (Thus in a patient with SLE who develops dyspnea/edema, evaluate for these mechanisms with BNP, echo, ischemic workup, and consider myocarditis or pulmonary hypertension.)  Management (principles) - Acute decompensated HF:   - Stabilize: oxygen as needed, relieve congestion with IV loop diuretics, consider vasodilators for hypertensive pulmonary edema, inotropes or mechanical support if cardiogenic shock. - Chronic HFrEF (guideline‑directed therapy to reduce symptoms and mortality):   - Foundational: ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) preferred if tolerated, or ACE inhibitor/ARB; beta‑blocker; mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (e.g., spironolactone); SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin/empagliflozin).   - Diuretics for volume control as needed.   - Add device therapy when indicated: ICD for primary prevention, CRT for selected conduction abnormalities.   - Advanced therapies: left ventricular assist device or heart transplantation for refractory advanced HF. - HFpEF:   - Control blood pressure, treat comorbidities (AF, CAD, obesity, diabetes), diuretics for congestion; SGLT2 inhibitors have shown benefit in many patients. - Specific to SLE patients:   - Treat underlying SLE activity (immunosuppression for myocarditis/pericarditis) in coordination with rheumatology and cardiology.   - Address modifiable cardiovascular risks (statins, blood pressure control, smoking cessation). - General measures for all HF patients:   - Sodium/fluid counseling, supervised exercise/rehabilitation, vaccination, regular monitoring (weight, renal function, electrolytes), multidisciplinary care.  When to refer/seek urgent care - Worsening dyspnea at rest, hypotension, signs of low perfusion, rising creatinine with congestion, syncope, or arrhythmia → urgent ED/cardiology assessment.  Prognosis and follow‑up - Prognosis varies by cause, LVEF, comorbidities and response to therapy; regular follow‑up to optimize guideline‑directed therapies and monitor complications (renal dysfunction, arrhythmias, sudden death) is essential.
10|72:	Short answer Heart failure (HF) is a clinical syndrome in which structural or functional cardiac abnormality prevents the heart from pumping sufficient blood and/or causes elevated filling pressures, producing symptoms (dyspnea, fatigue, orthopnea, fluid retention) and signs (jugular venous distension, crackles, peripheral edema). You call it HF when typical symptoms/signs are present and objective evidence corroborates cardiac dysfunction (elevated natriuretic peptide or imaging showing structural/functional abnormality such as abnormal echocardiogram). HF is classified by left‑ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) into HFrEF (≤40%), HFmrEF (41–49%) and HFpEF (≥50%).  When to suspect and how to confirm - Suspect HF with progressive breathlessness, exercise intolerance, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, leg/abdominal swelling, sudden weight gain, or signs of congestion.   - Initial tests: BNP/NT‑proBNP (elevated supports HF), chest X‑ray, ECG.   - Confirm with transthoracic echocardiography (systolic/diastolic dysfunction, valvular disease, chamber size). Cardiac MRI is useful for myocarditis or infiltrative disease. Coronary angiography if ischemia suspected.  Common causes - Ischemic heart disease (coronary artery disease, prior MI) and long‑standing hypertension are the most common.   - Other causes: cardiomyopathies (dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive), valvular heart disease, arrhythmias, congenital heart disease, chronic lung disease/pulmonary hypertension, metabolic causes (thyroid disease, diabetes), toxins/drugs (alcohol, some chemotherapies), and severe anemia or renal disease.  How systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) can cause HF SLE increases HF risk through multiple mechanisms: - Myocarditis: immune‑mediated inflammation of myocardium → systolic dysfunction and cardiomyopathy. Acute myocarditis may present with new HF, arrhythmias, or cardiogenic shock. Cardiac MRI and biopsy can help when suspected.   - Pericarditis and pericardial effusion: recurrent or constrictive pericarditis can impair filling and cause HF symptoms.   - Valvular disease (Libman–Sacks/sterile vegetations): causes significant regurgitation or stenosis over time, producing volume/pressure overload.   - Accelerated atherosclerosis and thrombosis: chronic inflammation and antiphospholipid antibodies raise risk of premature coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction → ischemic HF. Antiphospholipid syndrome also causes coronary/valvular thromboses.   - Pulmonary hypertension from pulmonary vascular disease or chronic thromboembolic disease → right‑sided HF.   - Renal involvement and hypertension: lupus nephritis and steroid‑related hypertension/ metabolic syndrome produce volume overload and hypertensive heart disease.   - Medication and treatment effects: some immunosuppressants and long‑term steroids can worsen metabolic risk or have cardiotoxicity.  Management principles 1. General HF management (follow guideline‑directed medical therapy):      - Relieve congestion: loop diuretics (furosemide) for symptomatic fluid overload.      - Chronic disease‑modifying therapies for HFrEF: ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) or ACE inhibitor/ARB, beta‑blocker, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, and SGLT2 inhibitor as appropriate. Titrate to tolerated target doses.      - Treat comorbidities: optimize blood pressure, diabetes, lipids, treat arrhythmias, correct ischemia (revascularization if indicated). Device therapy (CRT/ICD) or advanced options (LVAD, transplant) for eligible patients with refractory HF.      - For HFpEF focus on controlling congestion, BP, and comorbidities; SGLT2 inhibitors may be beneficial.  2. SLE‑specific measures that reduce HF risk or treat SLE‑related cardiac injury:      - Treat active cardiac inflammation: suspected lupus myocarditis or severe pericarditis is treated promptly with immunosuppression (high‑dose glucocorticoids ± other immunosuppressants such as mycophenolate, azathioprine, cyclophosphamide or biologics) in consultation with rheumatology and cardiology.      - Manage pericarditis with NSAIDs/colchicine; steroids if refractory or when required for systemic SLE control. Constrictive pericarditis may require surgical pericardiectomy.      - Anticoagulate when antiphospholipid syndrome or intracardiac thrombus present; manage thrombotic risks aggressively.      - Treat valvular disease surgically or percutaneously if severe and symptomatic.      - Control traditional cardiovascular risks: aggressive lipid management, smoking cessation, BP control, and careful steroid use to limit metabolic side effects.      - Avoid or monitor potentially cardiotoxic drugs; screen periodically (ECG, echo, biomarkers) if high risk.  Monitoring and follow up - Regular clinical assessments, weight monitoring, natriuretic peptides as indicated, and periodic echocardiography. In SLE patients, coordinate care between rheumatology and cardiology; escalate immunosuppression promptly for myocarditis or severe pericarditis.  Bottom line Heart failure is diagnosed when compatible symptoms/signs are supported by objective cardiac dysfunction. SLE can cause HF via myocarditis, pericardial disease, valvular lesions, accelerated ischemia/thrombosis, pulmonary hypertension, and renal/hypertensive mechanisms. Management combines standard HF therapies plus targeted treatment of the underlying SLE process (immunosuppression, anticoagulation, rheumatology collaboration) and aggressive control of cardiovascular risk factors.
